items.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
items.summary: Masked Israeli settlers attacked a European diplomatic delegation in the West Bank, injuring a visiting French mayor and damaging a consular vehicle. The incident drew sharp condemnation from European and Israeli officials and prompted renewed Belgian calls for European Union sanctions.

also.author: Aaron Boxerman and Adam Rasgon

also.note: The New York Times includes Palestinians alongside European officials directly in the headline, emphasizing a broader shared target rather than focusing exclusively on diplomats.

also.author: Azam Ahmed
also.title: Israeli Settlers Attack Palestinians and Washington Post Journalist in West Bank
also.note: The New York Times centers the headline on the preceding attack against Palestinians and an American Washington Post journalist rather than the European diplomatic delegation.

brief.what: Masked Israeli settlers attacked a European diplomatic convoy in the West Bank village of Taybeh, assaulting a French mayor with iron bars and smashing a Belgian consulate vehicle's window.
brief.who: The main actors include European envoys from Belgium, France, Poland, and the Catholic Church, masked Israeli settlers, French mayor Bernard Baudoux, and Israeli and Belgian government officials.
brief.context: The delegation visited the area to assess conditions following near-daily settler assaults targeting Palestinians attempting to gather their annual olive harvest, occurring one day after another attack injured a US photographer.
brief.why: The diplomats were monitoring the harvest area when settlers confronted them, with Baudoux alleging the attack demonstrated Israeli government tolerance for settler violence. Conversely, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office claimed reports may be part of a coordinated smear campaign against Israel, and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar noted the visit lacked prior coordination with the military.
brief.next: Israeli police and forensic investigators are conducting an inquiry into the incident, while Belgium announced it will continue advocating for European Union sanctions against violent settlers and their supporters.

brief.who: Pope Leo XIV is the head of the Catholic Church. Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke with him by phone regarding the war in Ukraine.
brief.context: The Pope underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth, and his doctors reported steady improvement via blood tests and X-rays. While hospitalized, he held a phone call with President Putin urging dialogue and peace, and appealed for a humanitarian ceasefire in the shelled Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy.
brief.why: The discharge followed medical findings from his doctors confirming steady improvement following the successful removal of the lung lobe.
brief.next: The Pope plans to lead the Angelus prayer on Sunday in St Peter's Square, while remaining tests to determine if the cancer spread have yet to be announced ahead of a planned November trip to Latin America.

brief.what: Chancellor John Healey reaffirmed that constructing a third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, expanding flight capacity from a capped 480,000 to 720,000 annually under an estimated £33bn project.
brief.who: Key figures include Chancellor John Healey, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Heathrow chief executive Thomas Woldbye, and the Department for Transport.
brief.context: The expansion has faced decades of debate and opposition over home demolitions and environmental disruption, with project completion already delayed from 2035 to 2039 due to planning and regulatory hurdles.
brief.why: Healey and Woldbye argue that expanding the airport bolsters national jobs, growth, and supply chains across the UK, whereas Burnham voiced skepticism by calling it a matter for Londoners to decide.
brief.next: The Department for Transport is reviewing public consultation feedback to decide on next steps, while Heathrow's owners require explicit backing from Burnham before year-end to proceed.

items.title: Accounts diverge over who ordered limits on Ukraine’s Starshield service
items.author: Clement Charpentreau
items.summary: Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite network was partially restored after speed caps disrupted drone operations. Conflicting accounts remain over whether the limits were ordered by the White House or the US military.

also.author: Ryan Mac
also.title: What Is Starshield, SpaceX’s Military-Grade Satellite Internet Service Ukraine Relies On?
also.note: The New York Times focuses on explaining the Starshield technology and Ukraine's operational reliance on it rather than reporting on the dispute over the operational restrictions.

brief.what: Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite communications service was at least partly restored after an unannounced speed cap of 160 kilometers per hour disrupted Ukrainian drone operations. Reports differ on whether the cap has been completely lifted or remains at the 160 km/h threshold.
brief.who: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk stated limits are determined by the US military and president, while UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth assured him access was restored. Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for limits to be removed.
brief.context: Starshield is the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite system, owned and controlled by the US government. The 160 km/h limit sits below the 300 to 400 km/h speeds of Russia's Geran-4 drones, hindering Ukraine's interceptor drones from chasing them.
brief.why: Reuters reported via officials that the restriction order originated inside the White House, though an anonymous senior US official denied the president made such a request. US President Donald Trump had criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel refineries for raising oil prices, following his declaration of an energy ceasefire.

items.summary: Several people have died or suffered injuries following a major fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta. Reports indicate the fire began when a live-fire training exercise struck a gas line amid intense wind gusts.

also.title: ‘Serious incident’ at Canada military base causes deaths, injuries
also.note: Al Jazeera quotes official phrasing by labeling the event a 'serious incident' rather than leading directly with a major fire.

brief.what: Several people were killed or injured after a major fire erupted at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta. Canadian network Global News reported that at least seven people died and dozens were injured, leading regional medical facilities to initiate high-casualty disaster protocols.
brief.who: Defence Minister David McGuinty announced the active situation, while Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith addressed the affected armed forces. Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh and emergency doctor Warren Thirsk coordinated the local response for the casualties.
brief.context: Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is the primary facility for Canadian military live-fire exercises, typically hosting about 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers on a standard day. Neighbouring provinces deployed resources to Alberta as an Edmonton hospital declared a code orange to manage incoming patients.
brief.why: Global News reported, citing unnamed military sources, that the fire began when a live-fire training exercise struck a gas line or gas well. The Municipal District of Wainwright stated that wind gusts of up to 100km/h (62mph) subsequently drove the fire through the base fences.

items.title: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base
items.author: The Associated Press
items.summary: A deadly incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta triggered a major fire that killed and injured military personnel and overwhelmed regional hospitals. Severe winds spread the fire into surrounding areas before municipal officials brought it under control.

also.author: Ian Austen
also.title: Deadly ‘Incident’ at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright Sparks Fire
also.note: The New York Times places 'incident' in quotation marks, emphasizing the unknown nature of what initially occurred on the base rather than leading with the resulting blaze.

brief.what: A deadly incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright sparked a major fire that spread across rural Alberta, leaving people killed and injuring a large number of military personnel. The disaster quickly overwhelmed regional healthcare facilities and forced the precautionary early closure of two advance voting polling locations.
brief.who: Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty announced the casualties and confirmed that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating, as emergency personnel and hospital staff across Edmonton treated incoming patients.
brief.context: Located near a town of about 7,000 residents, CFB Wainwright serves as one of Canada's primary combat training installations and hosts the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre for realistic battlefield exercises.
brief.why: Officials reported that a fire started in an on-base training area and was whipped out of control by severe wind gusts reaching up to 100 kilometres an hour, although the specific trigger of the deadly incident remains under official investigation.
brief.next: The Municipal District of Wainwright reported the fire was being held, while Defense Minister McGuinty stated authorities expect to release further information as the inquiry proceeds.
